lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Is this justice, Pluto? I die at thirty, while Thucritus—that old fossil past ninety—is still alive?

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Perfect justice, Terpsion. He is alive without praying for any of his friends to die. You spent the whole time plotting against him, waiting for the inheritance.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: But surely an old man, who can’t even use his money anymore, ought to leave life and make room for the young.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: That is a new statute, Terpsion: anyone too old to enjoy his money must die. Fate and Nature have arranged the matter otherwise.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Then I object to the arrangement. It ought to go in order: the oldest first, then the next in age, and so on. No reversals. No keeping some decrepit relic alive with three teeth left, barely able to see, bent double over four servants, nose full of snot, eyes full of rheum, past every pleasure, a breathing tomb laughed at by the young—while the handsomest, strongest young men die. That is rivers running uphill. Or at the very least we ought to know when each old man is going to die, so we don’t waste our attentions on the wrong ones. As it is, just like the proverb, the cart often carries off the ox.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: These things are managed much more sensibly than you think, Terpsion. And what is wrong with all of you, gaping after other people’s property and practically adopting yourselves into the households of childless old men? That is why you become a public joke when you get buried before they do. People enjoy it enormously. The more you pray for them to die, the sweeter it is for everyone when you die first. You have invented a remarkable new profession: falling in love with old women and old men—especially if they are childless. The ones with children are quite unattractive to you. And plenty of your beloveds have seen through the business model. Even when they do have children, they pretend to hate them, just so they can have admirers too. Then, when the wills are opened, the old bodyguard of flatterers is shut out, and the child—nature, in other words—wins everything, as is proper. The rest of you stand there grinding your teeth, fleeced clean.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: That is true enough. Thucritus, at least, ate his way through a fortune of mine, always seeming about to die. Whenever I came in, he would groan, then make some tiny little chirp from deep inside him, like an undercooked chick in an egg. So naturally I thought he would be climbing into the coffin any minute, and I kept sending gifts—lavish ones, so my rivals in love wouldn’t outbid me. Most nights I lay awake with worry, counting everything up and planning the next move. That is what killed me, in fact: insomnia and anxiety. And he, after swallowing all that bait, stood over my grave the other day laughing.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Well done, Thucritus. Live as long as possible—rich, and laughing at men like this. Do not die until you have escorted every last flatterer out ahead of you.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: Actually, Pluto, I would enjoy that now—if Chariades dies before Thucritus too.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Take heart, Terpsion. Pheidon and Melanthus as well—in fact all of them—will go before him, under the same anxieties.

lines.speaker: Terpsion
lines.text: I approve. Long life to you, Thucritus.
